notes: Scope: BASS (PSI-26), BASS-II (PSI-25) and the five SoFIE investigations (GEL, MIST, NCA, RTDFS, SMuRF), plus one umbrella record "SoFIE" for the project and facility. PSI lists only BASS and BASS-II; R/psi-access.md records that SoFIE is not in PSI under that name as of 2026-11-14, so the SoFIE records have psi_id null.

Every quote was checked verbatim against its text_file with the same normalisation as tools/quotecheck.py. Quotes from slide decks and two-column papers are sometimes fragments, because pdftotext interleaves columns; a fragment was used only where it is one unbroken run of the saved text.

raw/pdf/20210011385.txt is the full text that NTRS itself extracted from TM-20210011385.pdf (links.fulltext), not a local pdftotext run: the PDF is 48,972,416 bytes, over the 20 MB limit, so it was not downloaded. Page headers such as "NASA/TM-20210011385 14" sit inside that text and quotes avoid crossing them.

Files added for this family: raw/pdf/<id>.pdf and .txt for NTRS 20140011099, 20150008961, 20150008962, 20150019858, 20160000593, 20160012691, 20200000361, 20205004657, 20240007628, 20210022932, 20150023467, 20140004923, 20190033433; four PSI-26 documents fetched by file id as raw/pdf/PSI-26_*.pdf and .txt; nine nasa.gov pages as raw/nasa/solids-*.txt (HTML in raw/nasa/html/); NTRS and nasa.gov search responses in raw/ntrs/_search_solids/. Fetch logs: raw/pdf/_fetchlog_solids.jsonl and raw/nasa/_fetchlog_solids.jsonl. No request failed.

SoFIE-GEL is the only SoFIE investigation with published flight results in the sources found (NTRS 20240007628 and NASA pages). The extinction numbers come from Table 1 of that paper; the column meaning (flow cm/s, Reynolds number, strain rate 1/s, O2 %, pressure atm, conductive heat loss W/cm2) is read from the table header in the saved text.

SoFIE-MIST: no flight result with numbers was found on NTRS or nasa.gov (searches saved under raw/ntrs/_search_solids/; NASA pages only describe operations in 2024 and plans for Expedition 73). Its findings are from the 2013 grant summary (ground tests and simulation) and the 2015 Researcher's Guide, and are marked normal-gravity test, model or review.

SoFIE-NCA: no flight date and no flight result found. Findings are from the 1-g Narrow Channel Apparatus papers (NTRS 20140004923, 20190033433), marked normal-gravity test. The thick-slab microgravity data that NCA is compared against were taken in BASS-II and are filed under BASS-II.

SoFIE-RTDFS: one flight observation found (a NASA image caption of March 2025, no oxygen percentage or spread rate). Other findings are theory statements from NASA pages and the RTDFS precursor tests flown in BASS-II (reported in the BASS-II summary report).

SoFIE-SMuRF: no flight date and no flight result found; years is null. Findings are from the 2019 SoFIE project slides, the Researcher's Guide and the normal-gravity blowoff study that complements the BASS-II rod tests.

The findings filed under "SoFIE" are background statements from the 2015 Researcher's Guide and the NASA SoFIE page that motivate the project; they summarize earlier low-gravity research and are not SoFIE flight results (evidence_level "review or summary").

Disagreements between NASA sources, kept as found: (1) PMMA rod negative oxygen margin of safety: 2.4% O2 on the 2014 BASS-II poster (NTRS 20160000593), 1.4% O2 on the 2019 SoFIE slides (NTRS 20200000361). (2) Opposed-flow spread on PMMA rods: the 2014 poster says 1-g tests have higher spread rates than microgravity; the 2021 summary report says spread in microgravity is appreciably faster than in 1 g. (3) Nomex: a Nomex III sample propagated a flame at 22% O2 in BASS, while the three Nomex samples in BASS-II did not ignite. (4) BASS-II airflow: PSI and the 2014 poster approach text say up to 40 cm/s, the summary report says about 55 cm/s with no restrictors. (5) GEL sphere: "40 cm-dia" on the 2019 slide, 4-cm-diameter in the 2024 paper. (6) SoFIE launch: Northrop Grumman 17th resupply mission (February 2022 feature) versus "Launch July 5, 2022" on science.nasa.gov.

Ventilation shutdown: BASS and BASS-II recorded several flames that went out when flow was cut (within 2 s for a thin PMMA film), yet the Researcher's Guide lists "a fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off" as a misconception, reports that a local suppressant jet sustained a BASS flame with ambient airflow off, and GEL recorded about 15 minutes of pulsating flame at about 0.4 cm/s in elevated oxygen. decision_hint fields therefore treat shutdown as a first step to verify, not a guarantee.
BASS-II test dates: the PSI experimental table carries test dates in 2014, 2016 and 2018. They are reported as found and were not cross-checked against crew timelines.

Not included: Confined Combustion (NTRS 20205004657), a later ISS experiment that reused the BASS duct with baffles; its text is saved at raw/pdf/20205004657.txt for whoever covers it. BASS-M (Milliken textiles, described in the BASS fact sheet) is outside the named family and has no results in the sources read.
earth_instinct and decision_hint are interpretation written for VESTA, not NASA text. All conditions values are taken from the cited source; null means the source does not state it.

investigations.name: BASS
investigations.hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG); slightly modified Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) hardware: a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) with a variable speed fan, igniter and a small nitrogen nozzle
investigations.years: PSI investigation dates 10-01-2009 to 06-30-2013; ISS operations started March 2012; the first row of the PSI experimental table is dated 3/30/2012
investigations.pi: Paul Ferkul (PI); Sandra Olson (Project Scientist / Co-I, NASA GRC); James T'ien (Co-I, CWRU); Fumiaki Takahashi (Co-I)
investigations.objectives: (1) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity, using thicker, realistic fuels and wake flames. (2) Assess an inert gaseous extinguishing agent (nitrogen) on flames over different materials, geometries, preheating and flow.
fuels: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric blend (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass)
PMMA solid spheres, 1 and 2 cm diameter
candles in a ceramic tube: paraffin wax and Japan wax
investigations.sample_geometry: 41 fuel samples in three categories: flat, solid spheres, and candles within tubes. Thin flat samples 12 cm long by 1 and 2 cm wide; thick flat samples 5 cm long by 1 cm wide by 1 and 2 mm thick; spheres 1 and 2 cm in diameter; candles in a ceramic tube 6 mm in diameter by 25 mm long.

conditions.o2_percent: 17% to 21.5% (cabin air); nitrogen vitiation down to 16% O2 if desired
conditions.flow: fan-driven duct flow up to 40 cm/s, opposed or concurrent (fact sheet protocol: 5 to 50 cm/s)

investigations.variables: Airflow speed was the main variable; also flow direction (opposed or concurrent), fuel thickness, fuel preheating, nitrogen dilution, and a nitrogen suppressant jet supplied from 0 to 500 cc/min.
measurements: video camera (flame appearance, behavior)
digital still camera (spread rate, extinction dynamics)
radiometer (flame output)
anemometer (duct flow rate)

findings.earth_instinct: A tiny flame on a solid goes out by itself within seconds.

findings.topic: flare-up when airflow increases
findings.claim: A small flame is not particularly hazardous while it stays small, but it might flare up if air convection is suddenly increased or if it spreads into another fuel source.

findings.topic: nitrogen can strengthen a flame
findings.claim: The Researcher's Guide reports that early BASS results demonstrated nitrogen applied to the flame can strengthen it, through entrainment of oxygen by the suppressant stream.
findings.quote: Depending on the geometry of the flame and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle), it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. findings.earth_instinct: Any extinguishing gas aimed at a flame weakens it.

findings.topic: where to aim the suppressant

findings.earth_instinct: Opening things up and ventilating is the safe move once the flames look small.

findings.topic: flow cut-off extinguishes a thin PMMA flame within 2 s

findings.decision_hint: Make ventilation shutdown the first response to a fire alarm in microgravity: for this thin film it alone ended the flame in seconds. Verify extinction afterwards, since NASA lists self-extinction on ventilation shutoff as a misconception for fires in general.

findings.topic: extinction flow velocity for thin PMMA films
findings.claim: For thin PMMA films the opposed-flow extinction velocities were about 1 cm/s for 100, 200 and 300 micrometer thickness and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 micrometers.
findings.quote: When tests are repeated with samples of different thicknesses, the extinction velocities are found to be about 1 cm/s for 100, 200, and 300 μm and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 μm.

findings.decision_hint: A residual flow of roughly 1 cm/s was enough to keep these thin-film flames alive; ventilation shutdown has to bring local flow below that, so account for fans, leaks and crew motion.

findings.topic: extinction velocity rises as oxygen falls
findings.claim: At about 16 percent O2 the extinction velocities were about 2.6 cm/s (100 micrometer film) and about 4 cm/s (200 micrometer film); the report concludes the extinction velocity increases significantly as O2 is reduced and is independent of fuel thickness.
findings.quote: Tests were also conducted at a lower O2 level of about 16 percent for two different thicknesses and the extinction velocities were found to be about 2.6 cm/s for 100 μm and about 4 cm/s for 200 μm. It should be mentioned that the width of the sample was different, 20 mm for the 100-μm sample and 10 mm for the 200-μm sample. Even though there is insufficient data at the lower O2 level, it is clear that the extinction velocity significantly increases as the O2 level is reduced and is independent of the fuel thickness.

source.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

conditions.flow: about 2.6 and about 4 cm/s at extinction

findings.decision_hint: Lowering oxygen and lowering airflow work together: in a diluted atmosphere a flame quenches at a higher residual flow, so combine both when possible.

findings.topic: flame turns fully blue and vanishes before radiative extinction
findings.claim: As the opposed flow was gradually reduced, the thin-film flame shrank, lost its orange color and became completely blue.
findings.quote: As the flow speed is gradually reduced from about t = 27 s, the flame size starts shrinking and the orange color disappears and the flame becomes completely blue, most possibly because of the temperature drop brought about by radiative losses, which is enhanced by the increased residence time at low flow velocity.

findings.earth_instinct: No yellow flame means the fire is out.

findings.topic: negative oxygen margin of safety for PMMA rods
findings.claim: The 1-g blowoff limit for the 1/4-inch PMMA rod is at 16% oxygen, while BASS-II obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen: a negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4% O2, so normal-gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.

findings.earth_instinct: A material that passes the ground flammability test at a given oxygen level is safe at that level in space.

findings.topic: extrapolating the blowoff line to zero stretch
findings.claim: The authors suggest linearly extrapolating blowoff data to zero stretch rate as a conservative estimate of the minimum oxygen concentration at which the material burns; the y-intercept of their fit was 13.3% O2 against a minimum test point of 13.6% O2.
findings.quote: The linear blowoff boundary has interesting implications in that it may be possible to linearly extrapolate blowoff data down to zero stretch rate and use that oxygen value as a conservative estimate of the minimum oxygen concentration where the material will burn. This will allow us to de-rate materials based on normal gravity flammability tests to ensure the material will not burn in space. Using the y-intercept of the linear fit (13.3 % O2 in the Figure 4 fit, versus the minimum test point of 13.6 % O2) would add a slight level of conservatism.
